author: Kirby Wilson
title: Hillsborough overspent by $279 million, Florida CFO says - NewsBreak
text:
By Kirby Wilson ,
10 hours ago Florida Chief Financial Officer Blaise Ingoglia speaks during a news conference Wednesday in Brandon. Ingoglia said that Hillsborough County had overspent by more than a quarter billion dollars in the last five years alone. [ LUIS SANTANA | Times ] In the last half decade, Hillsborough County has overspent on services to the tune of more than a quarter billion dollars, Florida Chief Financial Officer Blaise Ingoglia said Wednesday.
At a news conference in Brandon, Ingoglia laid out the state’s case against recent local spending in the Florida county that’s home to Tampa. Ingoglia is heading up the Florida’s DOGE effort, which seeks to identify what it calls waste, fraud and abuse in spending.
“The taxpayers of this county should be outraged at the level of property taxes they are putting into the public coffers, only for it to be wasted by bureaucrats and career politicians,” Ingoglia said.
His office found that over the past five years, Hillsborough’s budget contained millions of dollars in excesses. They arrived at the calculation by starting with Hillsborough’s 2019-2020 general fund budget, which pays for much of the county’s operating expenses. Officials then projected how much the county’s budget should have increased during the next five years, based on inflation and population growth.
Florida Chief Financial Officer Blaise Ingoglia speaks during news conference in Brandon. [ LUIS SANTANA | Times ] Ingoglia’s team also allowed for millions more in what he characterized as typical government inefficiencies. Tabulators then compared the final projected number to Hillsborough’s actual 2025 budget. They found that Hillsborough had spent nearly $279 million more than necessary.
The county’s overall general fund budget for 2025 is $2.4 billion.
Ingoglia did not provide specific examples of wasteful spending. Those are coming later, he said.
Hillsborough County Commissioner Harry Cohen, a Democrat, said the county has a strong credit rating and spends wisely “on infrastructure, on resilience, on transportation — and of course, on public safety.”
Cohen said the lack of specifics made it difficult to respond to Ingoglia’s announcement.
“Unfortunately, we don’t have any details about what spending has been identified as being wasteful,” he said in a phone call Wednesday. Later, he added, “publishing numbers to convince people that there’s waste is different than actually explaining what that number is.”
Ingoglia said his team did not intend to perform a “full forensic audit” of each county’s finances. It’s not attempting to account for every misspent dollar. Instead, workers with DOGE — patterned after President Donald Trump’s Department of Government Efficiency — are crafting these projections and pulling a few select examples of items they find to be wasteful.
When the state releases its report detailing examples of excessive spending, county commissioners will work to address those issues, Cohen said.
Hillsborough property tax revenue increased about 74% in the last half decade, county documents show. In that time, some areas of spending have risen more quickly than others.
The county saw a 91% increase in public safety spending from all county funds between 2019 and 2025. It saw even greater proportional increases in health spending, infrastructure projects and economic development, the budget documents show. (While Ingoglia’s analysis included only property tax spending, these figures include all county revenue sources.)
Ingoglia acknowledged that reasonable people can disagree about what is considered wasteful spending.
“A lot of it is subjective,” he said of local government spending. “What becomes the test of what is a poor choice of taxpayer dollars, and what is a noble expenditure?”
That question, Ingoglia said, should be decided at the ballot box — both on a planned referendum on property taxes next fall, and by voting local officials out of office.
Gov. Ron DeSantis appointed Ingoglia to the chief financial officer post in July. Since taking office, Ingoglia has argued that Florida property taxes are too high in part because of wasteful spending by local governments. In similar announcements earlier this month, he said that Orange County and the city of Jacksonville each had budgets about $200 million fatter than necessary.
Florida Chief Financial Officer Blaise Ingoglia as a billboard is seen with a quote from the Tampa Bay Times. [ LUIS SANTANA | Times ] The push for fiscal scrutiny comes as DeSantis pushes for a 2026 property tax ballot referendum to address the increasing cost of home ownership in Florida. Although the governor has not offered a specific proposal, he’s railed against property taxes as a general concept in recent days.
“Truly owning your own home means your property shouldn’t be a piggy bank for local governments to extract revenue,” DeSantis posted to X Tuesday. “Homestead properties of Florida residents should be exempt from property taxes.”
